areas of machine learning, where computer systems automatically develop predictive
models for their input data. Despite their accomplishments to date, deep neural
networks are still dependent on human input, with key aspects of their design and
structure determined by carefully selected data sets and algorithmic techniques.
For a true quantum computer to be effective in this area, it would need to be able
to process complex multidimensional data directly from its surroundings, where
the difference between classical and quantum data can significantly impact the
performance of future quantum machines. Consequently, we must modify our current
notion of data accessibility. For instance, we no longer view images of clothing
from a specific style label as a single entity but rather as a collection of
sophisticated spectral patterns. Our goal is to outline the foundational
principles that will govern the creation of quantum machines capable of
automatically developing reliable models for complex data patterns. This study
investigates the underlying data structure that a quantum computer will use to
process its environment. We analyze the implications of a quantum machine being
capable of processing data that is inherently non-Clifford in nature. Our work
appears to be the first to systematically explore the data structure of quantum
machines. We have also discovered a novel, significant effect that arises from the
data's non-Clifford properties and found that this phenomenon can be utilized

This research introduces a tool that translates ACL2 to a subset of C, referred to as ACL2c. A C to ACL2 reasoner was developed in 2007 by Clayton and Capretto and this current project utilizes that reasoner to translate high-level C code into certified, ACL2 proof-dependent C code. A C parser was selected to generate the ACL2c code, incorporating optimizations for efficiency. Due to the complex nature of parsing all C code, a restricted subset of C is targeted for translation into ACL2c. A proof-generated C code generator has significant implications, including the potential for automated formal verification of general C programs using ACL2. This capability would allow for the certification of programs written in a safer subset of C as well as proving properties of large, open-source C programs. A major advantage of this generator is its ability to produce ACL2c code from unoptimized, intermediate C representations, thereby avoiding proof generation complexities. The full implementation details of this project, including the source code, is publicly available on GitHub at the following URL: https://github.com/RenditionSolutions/ACL2c-ProofGenerating-C-Code.

Investigations of the (39991) Iochroma system, comprised of a planet and a binary star component, have enabled a detailed analysis of the gravitational influence of the binary star on the planet's orbital path. Research has shown that a change in the binary star's eigenfrequency of rotational vibration correlates with the period of a planet's closest approach to the binary's central body. Moreover, findings indicate that a planet's orbital eccentricity is a reliable indicator for categorizing objects that have experienced a diverse range of distant interactions with binary systems. Additionally, the data support the presence of two distinct resonance types: type-III scalings, associated with a planet's rotational state, and a clustering of weak resonances stemming from a binary star's orbital eccentricity.

Building on Ramanujan's work with odd zeta values, we establish a formula using the Hurwitz zeta function, after first proving a more general result involving specific values of odd zeta functions. We then explore connections between these results and the properties of central binomial coefficients and central trinomial coefficients.

We demonstrate in this note that the elliptic cohomology ring elliptic cohomology elliptic cohomology is isomorphic to the cohomology ring cohomology ring cohomology when the group G operates trivially on V. Specifically, this involves considering G operating on the complex vector space V, which results in G operating on the complex projective space CP(V). The elliptic cohomology ring then enables us to construct a circle equivariant ring circle equivariant that captures the Chow ring cohomology of the quotient V / Z, for any integer Z.

The goal of this project is to apply the principles of algebraic topology to study physical systems through the use of machine learning tools. Topology, a branch of mathematics focused on the study of spatial relationships, offers a rich and comprehensive approach that can be applied to a wide variety of physical systems. By implementing machine learning techniques, researchers can create more efficient and accurate tools for analyzing and understanding the topology of complex materials, such as fractional quantum Hall states and other novel phases of matter. The key challenges in this field involve developing methods for analyzing and learning topological data, as well as integrating these approaches into existing physics frameworks. The project will investigate three main areas of focus: (1) representing topological data in an efficient and standardized format, (2) reducing the computational cost of algebraic topology for large-scale systems, and (3) integrating machine learning techniques into a well-established physics framework used to study topological materials.

This paper provides a comprehensive, next-to-leading-order examination of the angular distributions in $J/\psi$ production through $e^{+}e^{-} \to J/\psi + \eta_c, \chi_{cJ}$ ($J=0,1,2$) by examining the $J/\psi\gamma^*$ decay. The analysis reveals that certain non-relativistic QCD predictions, including those on colour octet components and $J$-matrix elements, are consistent with observed magnitudes and signs. Notably, our study includes a leading-order diagram contribution missing in previous studies and calculates all relevant next-to-leading-order diagrams. The examination also positions us to perform a final, next-to-leading-order angular analysis and determine the absolute magnitudes of $J/\psi$ colour octet components.

Our online survey with 235 Signal users revealed that users can be categorized into two groups: those who are fully informed and those who are unsure of how Signal works with PINs. Our qualitative research interviewed 13 users and found that the uncertain group may lack understanding of Signal's security features. Additionally, we found that the enthusiastic group, who were fully informed, were eager to share their security knowledge with others. Our study provides new insights from user interviews that can inform the development of more informative and transparent security methods for Android apps.

This study presents a method for efficiently calculating the solar energy absorbed per unit area by incorporating the solar irradiance into a Gaussian quadrature formula, resulting in a straightforward calculation. The resulting rule provides high accuracy for integrating functions with complex modulations, particularly those involving diurnal and seasonal temperature variations. The solar-weighted Gaussian quadrature formula can be used to model the heat flux associated with long-wave radiation, and the applied surface boundary condition in solar and planetary climate simulations. The formula enables the separation of spatial and temporal variability in solar energy, permitting independent calculations of intensity and distribution. The method was tested on several example functions, including irradiance models and a model of the atmospheric mass distribution. The results showed a high degree of accuracy, with relative errors less than 0.0005 percent for a moderate number of points. The method was more efficient than other numerical integration techniques, requiring less computational time. The solar-weighted Gaussian quadrature formula was also generalized to other atmospheric models, including those with overlapping zones and stretched grids. The method was more convenient to use than other numerical integration techniques, requiring minimal code modifications and no input limits on the grid size.

The curvature formed by the generalized Gauss-Newton matrix plays a significant role in the convergence rate of various algorithms used in optimization and machine learning. Unfortunately, computing this matrix is computationally expensive due to its large size and O(n^2) complexity. Formerly, such issues were addressed either by dividing the cost into smaller portions or approximating the curvature with a simplified model. Now, a new approach called ViViT viktormulti simplifies this in two ways: by reducing the curvature's dimensionality and smallening the complexity factor. The technique is versatile as it can be used alongside existing methods that address the cost issue or simplify the curvature's structure, thus enhancing performance. The technique is efficient as it only requires computing a subset of the curvature's entries, making it more suitable for large datasets. The effectiveness of the technique has been demonstrated through experiments on various deep learning models and datasets. The technique is available through https://github.com/mvrl/AutoMLTools.

Many languages distinguish nouns by grammatical gender, which influences how subjects are conjugated and how objects are recognized in sentences. Although the impact of gender on verb conjugation is well understood, its effect on noun representation remains a relatively under-researched topic. This study investigates how grammatical gender affects learning in low-resource, gender-labeling languages by manipulating pre-trained noun embeddings for different genders. It does this by analyzing a specific naming convention used in Demotric languages, which assign gender to each noun through suffixes or prefixes. Two methodologies were employed to examine gender distinction at the noun level. First, a binary classification task showed that the gender of noun labels given by speakers matched the expected gender for that noun in 62% of cases. Second, a numerical analysis on gender-labeling languages found a negative correlation between accuracy of predicted gender and accuracy of binary gender classification. Furthermore, speakers' numerical gender labels for nouns showed consistency with the suffixes of the nouns in question. These results suggest that grammatical gender may influence how people conceptualize and represent nouns. This study further reveals how grammatical gender can impact learning when the gender of noun labels given by speakers is utilized in an NLP model.

In our previous work, we proposed the concept of charmability, a generalised version of rigidity, for study. We then demonstrated that all non-compact, catenary arithmetic groups exhibit a particular type of charmability, known as charmability of the first kind. We further investigated the relationship between this form of charmability and another concept, the charmability of the second kind, in groups like SL2(Z[kh]), particularly when kh is an order in a quadratic field with class number two that has a prime class. We then defined an additional concept, charmability of the boundary, in the setting of Finsler geometry and proved that it correlates with the charmability of the group when the geodesic metric is used. Notably, our research discovered that the boundary of SL2(Z[kh]) is charmingly rigid, meaning it exhibits a particular type of charmability, under specific conditions.

Estimating the class-specific position of an object is crucial in numerous applications. In this study, we explore zero-shot, actuated object position estimation where the involved objects and actions are unknown. Each scene contains a single moving object, and our task is to predict its movement direction. Our proposed method employs a combination of image descriptors, expected action trajectories, and calculated angular disparities. The performance of our model is evaluated using the PAQUET dataset under two distinct simulation conditions. Additionally, we analyze how different descriptor networks impact results and assess the effects of dataset quality and size on model performance. Our findings indicate that a trained encoder using a specific network outperforms other alternatives, and the accuracy of position estimation improves with a larger, higher-quality dataset.

Urban planners face a significant challenge in managing the growing demand for
city infrastructure. To efficiently allocate resources, accurate and scalable
traffic forecasting is crucial, especially for key transportation routes. Current
spatial models, however, often rely on dense data, neglecting the potential of
other city areas. To address this limitation, we explore using temporal data.
Our approach identifies significant features in traffic time-series. To do this, we
first develop a system to detect rare, distinct patterns within time-series data.
Next, we refine these patterns into co-occurring features detected across the
city. Our results indicate that these features have a considerable impact on traffic
forecast accuracy. Furthermore, the extracted patterns can be utilized for spatial
interpolation, providing valuable insights for urban planners. Our findings are also
supported by a concrete case study.

This study introduces variational graph autoencoders (VAEs) integrated with directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) to address key challenges in statistics and machine learning, specifically under uncertainty and missing data conditions, as well as counterfactual questions arising from causal inference. VAEs, originating from the probabilistic perspective of inference, outperform traditional methods in these areas. Traditionally, VAEs have focused on continuous data, but the proposed algorithm, variational Autocomplete Embedding Graph Learner (VAEGL), handles both categorical and continuous information by representing variables using graphs and embedding them in a multidimensional space for further analysis. Building on existing work with structural recognition networks (SRNs), VAEGL improves upon SRNs by its ability to handle missing data, uncertainty, and Causal and Counterfactual inquiries. In addition to these advancements, for the proposed algorithm to function, learning the parameters of the graph (edges and nodes) is required, but existing algorithms have a limitation of either ignoring the graph structure or not being able to estimate it from data. Furthermore, to address this limitation, the proposed algorithm to learn the DAG is based on the structural SP-GNN method, but in the general case, this method has an exponential dependence on the number of variables. To overcome this problem, the proposed algorithm to address this problem is based on the SP-GNN method with the KL regularisation from SRN, but to further improve this, the proposed algorithm to address this

We introduce the Irish LOFAR facility's capture pipeline, a capture pipeline specifically designed to quickly process and store radio signals from transient events. The pipeline, known as REALTA, is in early stages but has shown promising results in both real-time and delayed processing modes. Its real-time capabilities match the LOFAR Real-time Transient Analysis pipeline's (LoTATIS) detection modes, with both systems operating during the 2021 GLEAM-DR2 survey. The REALTA pipeline has also demonstrated efficiency in processing archived data from previous events, showcasing its potential for storing triggered events in the future. The systems' real-time capabilities match the 10 minute lofar real-time dataset, with capture of events outside this time frame also possible using archived data. The system stores data on fast and regular radio signals in 16bit, in contrast to lofarrt, which stores unique event detections in binary normalised values. The system has also recorded typical spectra during the 2021 GLEAM-DR2 survey with capture of events in the frequency range of 30-43.5 MHz. The system has also recorded samples from 9 dedicated streams supporting the search for fast radio bursts from the FRB2020AAU stream. The system has also recorded 5 minute samples from a commissioning pipeline which displayed similarities with the well known FRB2014AGI stream. The system has also found possible candidate events in the search for fast radio bursts from 9 dedicated

We suggest the term 'clever metaphotonics' for optical systems where the size of both the structure dimensions and wavelength are in the same order, allowing for novel and efficient light management. By combining this with artificial intelligence, specifically through genetic algorithms, the search for optimal metaphotonics can be globally directed even in the presence of local minima. To illustrate the potential of clever metaphotonics, we demonstrate two designs for light control - for a laser and a tunable laser - showing their performance can be surpassed by their conventional counterparts in terms of efficiency and controllability.

The primary goal of this research is to track film industry trends. We've expanded our film dataset to date, covering films from 1999 to 2022, and aimed to pinpoint key factors influencing box office success. Our approach diverges from previous methods by focusing on films' actual usage duration instead of their initial duration. We also delve into the impact of pre-viewing on box office performance and examine the significance of meta-critic scores. Our findings indicate that shorter running times for newly released films are not indicative of declining box office success. Furthermore, we observed that higher quality, pre-viewed films do not generate more revenue. Finally, we determined that meta-critic scores have a significant, positive correlation with box office success.

The integration of widely distributed, diverse energy sources into the main grid has led to a significant decrease in voltage stability. To improve the system's resilience, we're proposing a method of controlling the power flow to maintain voltage stability without affecting the energy production. By modulating the power export of distributed generators, we can enhance the system's dynamics and protect it against small disturbance errors. To this end, we've developed a theoretical framework for stabilizing voltage behavior through the adjustment of power flow direction, determined by frequency modulation of the governors. Simulations reveal that this method can effectively increase the system's frequency stability and maintain voltage stability.

Cyber-physical networks need to be highly intelligent, resilient, and secure to accommodate cutting-edge cognitive systems. Intelligent networks and devices that learn and adapt will become crucial in various sectors, driving innovative applications. Our proposed framework and tools allow for the design, management, and optimization of these advanced networks and their interaction with learning entities to achieve specific objectives. This requires tackling intricate issues in dynamics, optimization, and topology, as well as ensuring secure and reliable communication systems. Our framework and tools, including the Model Transformer and the Neural Network Converter, enable the efficient handling of these challenges to unlock the full potential of cognitive systems. We demonstrate their capability through several relevant examples.

This is the second part of a study on partially polarized inverse Compton scattering, known as MAPPIES, and its influence on the spectra of certain celestial bodies. The model generates synthetic spectra that integrate the radiative processes of a target source, incorporating the effects of external radiation, non-thermal electron emissions, and external radiation reprocessing. It utilizes a Monte-Carlo framework to simulate particle interactions and has been enhanced for improved speed and precision. The updated code has been tested for modeling the spectra of certain celestial bodies, with particular focus on specific spectral features and radiative feedback effects. The results demonstrate that MAPPIES is effective in reproducing the dominant spectral segment of active galactic nuclei, including the UV/soft X-ray excess in BL Lac objects, although it falls short of accurately modeling the X-ray/TeV plateau in these objects. The model has also replicated the UV/soft X-ray excess in He1440+521, a highly variable object. The code has been made available for public download at the provided URL.

This research focuses on finding the conditions under which locally holomorphic extensions in complex topology can be generalized to complex surfaces. We begin by reviewing essential principles, including Baker-Campbell-Haussmann theorem, the Fel'd-Mahler theorem, and the underlying topological considerations, before examining the local properties of complex surfaces and their connection to Steiner chains via Gaudin Portraits. This serves as the foundation for our central theorem, which elaborates on the connection between the generating functions of holomorphic transformations and the Birkhoff-Gottlieb forms on the relevant complex surfaces. Furthermore, it provides generating functions for the n-fold monodromy transformations of a given Riemann surface, thereby extending analytical methods to complex surfaces of arbitrary dimension. To demonstrate the scope of this method, we evaluate the generating functions for the n-fold transformations of the elliptic genus on the total space of the Hirzebruch-Moore sigma model.

We investigate virtual experiments of state detection in a system with two components, focusing on states having specific mathematical properties. The system is comprised of a superposition of various states, each having identical structures. The detection process involves comparing the system to a reference state multiple times, with each iteration involving multiple interactions. For certain states with these specific mathematical properties, our model shows that the system's behavior becomes increasingly consistent as the number of interactions grows. In such cases, our model can accurately describe system behavior even without considering all possible variables, by applying a simplified mathematical framework that is consistent across multiple interactions. This simplified framework relies on a more basic and fundamental set of variables that remains consistent across multiple interactions. This phenomenon is not seen in systems that are random and unpredictable, and this consistent behavior can be leveraged to verify fundamental principles of quantum mechanics. Additionally, our research provides a method for virtually implementing measurements that have complex characteristics on realistic experimental setups. Our findings also highlight an important aspect of how fundamental principles of quantum mechanics can be accurately and thoroughly tested, and this could have significant implications on quantum simulation and quantum computing experiments.

Baryons are constructed through a quantization process of a QCD string that undergoes specific changes, resulting in the creation of three flavor quarks and an antisymmetric two-form field. This process occurs via two distinct mechanisms: string fragmentation and a phenomenon called'sliding alived by a shock, associated with an increase in the string's tension. Baryon formation can also be described by compositing certain bosonic structures in a quantum field theory, characterized by baryon collective motion based on three form variables.

The way seismic waves travel through the sun depends on its internal structure and any lateral changes in the speed of sound within the sun's core and radiative zone. Studies using helioseismic travel times have revealed complex movements in the sun's interior over a cycle of its 11-year activity change, and these movements affect seismic wave speed in the sun's core and outer core. To understand how activity affects seismic wave speed in different layers of the sun, researchers have broken down the effect of circular flow on seismic waves in terms of the mass of fluid involved. A study using 8 years of data from SOHO and TRACE observed the effect of circular flow on seismic waves in the sun's core and outer core, and it observed a significant decrease in travel times in the east-west direction but a smaller change in the north-south direction. This change in the north-south direction is due to a type of seismic wave with a specific oscillation frequency. When observing this type of wave, researchers found that circular flow does not affect seismic wave speed in the sun's core but it does in the outer core, however, when considering all types of waves in the sun's core, circular flow actually causes seismic wave speed to decrease, which is the opposite of what is observed during times of decreased activity in the north-south direction. This change in the effect of circular flow on seismic wave speed in the sun's core over time may be related to activity levels in the sun's outer layers, however,

Recent research has found that stochastic gravitational waves generated by random fluctuations in cosmic magnetic fields could be detectable via pulsar timing array experiments. To determine how detectable this signal is, we analyzed various parameters such as the redness of magnetic fields, their evolution speed, the critical density for magnetostatic reconnection, and the present-day strength of magnetic fields in galaxies. Our findings indicate that if magnetic fields in galaxies are highly correlated over large distances and their random fluctuations decrease at a slower rate, a significant portion of galaxies may contribute to a detectable signal. This would be particularly true if magnetic fields in galaxies are strong, with an average strength similar to our own galaxy. The predicted power spectrum of the gravitational signal may be accurately approximated using a simple equation that takes into account several key parameters, including magnetic fields' correlation length, their initial strength, and their evolution speed. This equation may serve as a useful reference for future research into possible contributions of magnetic fields to the gravitational signal.

Light field technology is currently a focal point of interest among researchers due to its exceptional 3D display and measurement capabilities. Nevertheless, the complexity of processing and compression required for analysis makes it a challenge. Past studies on light field compression have drawn from the experiences of researchers working on 2D image compression but have often failed to consider the unique characteristics of light field data. In this study, a practical approach to learning-based light field compression is presented from both the encoder and decoder perspectives. Initially, a disparity-aware model of the center token's distribution in light field subsets is proposed. This token distribution model can be used for both compression and the reconstruction of light field subsets. To enhance compression performance, a feature displacement model that reduces the correlation between displaced features in light field subsets is introduced. These models are trained solely using data sourced from an online portal where four-category refocused images are available for free. The results demonstrate the advantages of our solution over existing methods, showcasing up to a 63.9% improvement in PSNR, a 64.1% improvement in MS-SSIM, and equivalent or superior quality to state-of-the-art methods while experiencing a reduced model size. The source code for the proposed method has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/fengnuotian/lf-disp-model.

Research in cross-language information retrieval is crucial, especially when searching multilingual documents for specific information using a query in a different language. Two frameworks, interactive and non-interactive approaches, can be employed to solve this problem via translation methods. While interactive and non-interactive frameworks serve distinct purposes, they share common goals in retrieving relevant information from a search database, albeit with differing requirements and benefits. This research aims to explore and compare these two frameworks, examining their effectiveness, shortcomings, and significance in cross-language information retrieval. We analyze and discuss existing studies from two frameworks, focusing on key aspects such as search operation, query representation, document representation, similarity measurement, and data distribution. Our findings indicate that both frameworks can produce significant AUC values, suggesting significant implications for future CLIR research. We hope this review stimulates more investigations and contributions in both areas, ultimately leading to better performance in CLIR tasks.

In many low-income countries, weighted survey designs are used to gather reliable data on diverse population subsets, but the estimation process is often complicated by the inclusion of rare and rarest population subsets. This study proposes an innovative method for estimating rare population subsets in frequency-weighted surveys. The approach uses a larger sample dataset, combined with a designed statistical model, to enhance representation of these subsets. The research compares and tests this method with another established approach that uses a calculated weight profile. The results from two datasets, specifically Ghana's Sixth Round DHS and its Marital Status Microdata, showed that the proposed method yielded more accurate estimates for rare gender, age, and educational level subsets. This study finds that the calculated weight profile method can lead to overestimation of rare subsets when the underlying frequency distribution changes. In contrast, the proposed method is based on a fixed model, making it less prone to this issue. However, both methods have their own advantages and limitations, and the choice between them ultimately depends on the specific research goal and requirements. The study suggests that the proposed method offers a viable alternative for estimating rare population subsets and should be further utilized, especially in research contexts that rely on designed experiments.

We develop a quantum version of the Kelly criterion for optimal betting and risk management as a method to minimize the conditional variance of the player's wealth, given the outcome of an experiment with known probability. This formulation builds on previous work by Hiyama who investigated the quantum aspects of betting, but his method only applies to situations with only two possible outcomes. In this study, we explore betting scenarios with multiple possible outcomes and find that for experiments with certain dependencies between outcomes, the optimal betting strategies will involve both continuous and discrete quantum states being used simultaneously. By treating the player's wealth as a continuous variable, we find that its fluctuations can be represented by a positive semi-definite quadratic form, which has previously unexplored connections to the quantum mechanical observables associated with the experiment. This study also discusses how to translate risk management strategies from the classical world to the quantum world, with examples based on a recently described continuous variable model of a spin experiment.

Recently, researchers were able to predict the stacking-independent exciton of MoSiN4, which opened the door for the creation of two-dimensional semiconductor materials. Further investigation led to a broadened search for similar materials, resulting in the stacking-independent exciton being found in various structures: TiSiN4, TiGeN4, WSiN4, WSIN4, GePN6, GeAsN4, GeAsP2, and GeAsSe2. Through the use of calculations based on perturbation theory, it was noticed that the stacking-independent exciton has a tendency to move towards the top of the bandgap when the energy alignment of the semiconducting quasiparticles is strong and close to that of the stacking-dependent exciton. Conversely, a robust energy alignment can actually separate the on-top and under-gap states of different stacking configurations. The stacking-independent exciton's characteristics were found to be independent of the specific two-dimensional semiconductor material, yet the dependence on the type of stackings was observed, specifically in materials with a type-II stack. By employing the proposed alignment theory, it was also revealed that certain two-dimensional semiconductors, both with type-I and type-II stacks, could potentially exhibit both stacking-dependent and independent excitons within the same material.

A key objective of the LHCb experiment is to uncover the underlying cause of the unusually low occurrence rate of specific rare hadronic decay processes predicted by the Standard Model of physics. One such decay process is $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^+$, which is anticipated to manifest at the LHC due to the generation of $\Sigma^+$ mesons breaking up in hadronic interactions within the detector. Prior studies have established confidence in detecting rare decay processes such as $\Sigma^+ \to p e^+ e^-$. Similar to this known decay, the uncommon $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ decay is predicted to have a deep connection with the internal structural characteristics of the $\Sigma^+$ meson, thereby providing a unique means of extracting information about its composition. Assuming an energy level of $7$ TeV and a duration of $1$ femtobarn of data collection at the LHCb experiment, it has been determined that, upon applying a set of precise selection criteria designed to filter out background noise, the uncommon $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ decay process can be detected with a level of certainty of $3.574 \sigma$ in a study titled "Searching for the uncommon decay $\Sigma^+ \to p e^+ e^- ($including an alternative for $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$) at

A theoretical framework for the evolution of molecular cloud cores is presented, where the magnetic field and mechanical instability play key roles. Our analysis indicates that core disruption begins when gravitational forces outweigh magnetic effects, leading to the fragmentation of the core into smaller clusters, which eventually lose their internal magnetic fields, giving rise to protostellar systems. Our simulations of this process, using complex three-dimensional models of molecular cloud cores, reveal that cluster formation is rapid, with a timescale of approximately 15,000 years, and that these nascent stars typically have masses in the range of 1 to 25 solar masses. Our findings also suggest that cluster formation primarily results in the development of multiple, equally massive protostars, rather than a hierarchical structure of more and less massive stars, and that the orbital periods and eccentricities of these stellar orbits are substantial, with a maximum period of approximately 15 years and a maximum eccentricity of approximately 0.7. Our results predict a high rate of binary star formation and potential for the formation of multiple, aligned stellar orbits, which could impact the formation and properties of planets within these systems, particularly in regards to planetary spin, orbit, and satellite configuration.

Achieving accurate image reconstruction and spectral analysis across various wavelengths
and conditions depends on understanding and mitigating the effects of atmospheric scattering.
To do so, researchers must accurately model the atmosphere, but there's no universal definition
of atmospheric scattering. In this study, we examine and discuss different atmospheric models
used to simulate the effects of scattering, particularly focusing on two parameters: the Hermite
polynomial scale size of 0.56 cm at 500 nm and the scattering angle $\theta$. We also establish
a standard for measuring and reporting these parameters. By conducting on-sky observations using
a Shack-Hartmann sensor, we determined the equations for the variation of the scale size and theta
in terms of atmospheric conditions. Our results can inform the development of image reconstruction
techniques and scattering models for other applications. We find that the atmosphere exhibits four
distinct regimes based on the wind speed. In two of these regimes, the scale size correlates well with
pre-existing models, but changes significantly with wind speed in the other two. In all cases, the
atmospheric models' theta appear to be unaffected and can be accurately represented by a constant
expression. We propose a set of standard formulas for calculating the scale size and theta based on
the atmosphere's temperature and pressure. We believe that implementing these formulas will advance
high-precision applications and provide a more reliable foundation for understanding and modeling
atmospheric scattering.

This paper tackles the problem of modeling complex time sequences that contain multiple distinct components by using a condensed framework based on a sparse prediction model. We propose a novel approach to the task, referred to as Multi-term Decomposition for Multi-variable Time Series Modeling (MDTSTM). The core prediction mechanism of MDTSTM involves an efficient and flexible approach based on a factorized product of three vectors. We extend this model to handle multi-term temporal sequences by integrating a prior learned from data that accounts for similarities across related time points. The method makes use of a prior that condenses the characteristics of temporal sequences, known as latent vectors. It then assumes that time sequence elements are sparseely connected to these condensed vectors. We demonstrate that this method can automatically detect underlying patterns in data and find relevant earlier-time correlations. We show that both the near and far past temporal correlations can be identified without supplementary adjustments to the method. We evaluate the proposed method against other leading techniques with multiple real-world datasets. The results confirm that MDTSTM achieves superior performance, equivalent performance, or significant improvements over existing techniques. In particular, it achieves superior accuracy when modeling up to 5 previous time steps. Additionally, our method performs better than others when there are varying numbers of underlying patterns in data.

The 1939-1940 correspondence between Kolmogorov and Pontryagin marked a pivotal turning point in the development of topological groups and representations of groups. This interaction facilitated the introduction of the Pontryagin transform, a crucial extension of the Fourier transform, and the identification of Pontryagin duals, a pivotal, fundamental topological group theory concept. This paper presents a historical reflection on that pivotal correspondence and the integrated understanding of the Fourier transform and Pontryagin transform developed through it. Additionally, the paper proposes a continuous reasoning framework to the global geometric unitary representation theory of compact, abelian groups by extending and integrating ideas from the works of Pontryagin, Kolmogogorov, Gelfand, and Schwartz, with a focus on representing irreducible representations and the global geometric unitary representation theory of the one-dimensional form.

The increasingly popular Federated Learning (FL) method, driven by the need for privacy, has a crucial role for cross-device, cross-network, and cross-city data aggregation. Given the broad spectrum of FL applications, ensuring differential confidentiality is particularly challenging due to diverse data categories involved. We propose two confidential training strategies for FL: PDC-GDA (Privacy Preserving Gradient Descent with Convergence Analysis) and PDCLAF (Privacy Preserving Cross City Federated Learning). Both techniques leverage the distance-based method to estimate the training data spread, setting an upper bound for the attacker's data access. We conduct comprehensive fairness and convergence analyses on both methods to guarantee that the trained models remain consistent with local, regional, and global data distributions, while ensuring training convergence and improving test accuracy. Furthermore, we develop a framework to evaluate FL training confidentiality, using both natural language and image classification tests. Our results show that the PDC-GDA method maintains test accuracy within 0.9% of the original model, while the PDCLAF method achieves this with only 0.1% reduction in test accuracy, and both methods guarantee that the attacker's success probability is at most 16 in 17 attempts.

A proposed model of a supersymmetric model based on the $U(1)_X$ global symmetry is presented, where the symmetry is broken to a very small fraction of the SM value by introducing a small value for the $U(1)_X$ gauge symmetry, resulting in the appearance of two very light $U(1)_X$ gauge bosons. The emergence of these two massless gauge bosons is shown to be equivalent to two additional long-range forces acting alongside gravity and the electromagnetic force. The dark energy sector is represented by right-handed neutrinos which undergo a majorana mass conversion through a highly non-degenerate ratio of two to one with their counterpart supersymmetric partners, thereby contributing to the universe's present-day flatness. Consequently, these right-handed neutrinos, in conjunction with the additional non-Abelian nature of $U(1)_X$, are able to generate the universe's observed dark energy. The model's predictions indicate that these right-handed neutrinos, in a state of non-relativistic motion, possess masses less than about two tev in magnitude and with highly degenerate mass spectra. The model's additional predictions include the production of pairs of these right-handed neutrinos, along with $U(1)_X$ gauge bosons, by interacting with the supersymmetric partners of the SM model through highly degenerate mass spectra. The model's overall particle content is also shown to satisfy the correct relic abundance of dark energy as dictated by the universe's present

To boost the energy transfer rate in a wireless powered transfer network assisted by intelligent surface, we developed an innovative undervised machine learning technique that optimizes the energy transfer channel's reflective surface parameters. Break-in events caused by users with diverging transmission paths from the energy source disrupt the network's operation. Our proposed algorithm continuously monitors the energy transfer efficiency and updates the surface reflection parameters only when this efficiency drops below a certain threshold. The undervised machine learning technique excels in real-time operation, surpassing traditional convex optimization methods in average transfer efficiency. Moreover, it has the advantage of handling network disruptions and is more suitable for dynamic and diverse scenarios than traditional optimization methods.

For the first time, researchers used total absorption gamma spectroscopy to directly observe the two-neutron evaporation residue $^{186}$Hg following $4n$ quasi-fission in $^{190}$Pt. They found that the 0$^+$ ground state in $^{186}$Hg has an energy of 84.01(3) MeV, consistent with a previous study, but with improved precision. By combining this measurement with a previous $4n$ quasi-fission experiment, they calculated the half-life for $^{186}$Hg to be 19.6(4) seconds. Furthermore, they obtained a $B$(2$^+$) value of 0.89(17)%, indicating that the 2$^+$ isomer in $^{186}$Hg is formed with a high probability right after its production. Within the framework of a unified theory, where a single symmetry dictates matter-gauge interactions, research explores the interlinking of the 'dark substance' hypothesis with the mechanism of leptogenesis. This 'dark substance' hypothesis proposes that visible matter's mass origin stems from a dark sector's contribution, much like the universe's large-scale structure formation, driven by a dark proton's anomalous charge. A comprehensive investigation is conducted into the generation of lepton masses and lepton sector interactions by the dark sector's impact. It's shown that, under the influence of a dark neutron and a dark photon with non-standard properties, a prediction can be made for the dark neutron's Dirac/Majorana mass as $m_D \sim 2.4 \cdot 10^{-3}~\mathrm{eV} < m_n$ and the dark neutron's half-life as $\tau_n \sim 6 \cdot 10^3~\mathrm{seconds}$. This research also identifies a range for the dark proton's mass as $m_p \sim 2.4 \cdot 10^{-5}~\mathrm{eV}$ and the dark proton's half-life as $\tau_p \sim 8 \cdot 10^9~\mathrm{seconds}$. For optimal control problems involving physical systems, gathering complete system data can be a significant challenge due to its considerable size and complexity. In the absence of detailed model descriptions, advanced methods can be employed to identify essential system parameters. However, these methods typically require extensive training data, which may be difficult to obtain in certain scenarios. In this study, a novel approach is presented to efficiently obtain informative training data for optimal control problems through interactive user input. Specifically, we utilize user-provided feedback in the form of partial system information and inferences based on that information to enhance data quality and reduce training data size. We demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed method across various scenarios, including parameter estimation and control tasks, using virtual systems and real-world robotic applications involving a flying robot. Furthermore, we examine the user's role in our proposed framework and assess the effectiveness of different training data acquisition strategies.

In the context of the Toda conformal quantum field theory based on $\mathfrak{sl}_3[\hbar^{-1}\partial]$ as well as the Toda $\mathfrak{sl}_3$-FK conjugate modular invariant, a series of exact relationships known as the Ward identities are formulated that connect degeneracies of various partitions in the Toda conjugate modular invariants with respective character expansions of integrable highest component Verma modules for $\mathfrak{sl}_3[\hbar^{-1}(\partial + A(x))}$, where $A(x)$ represents a specific elliptic algebra element. These relationships specifically consider the principal specialization of the Toda conjugate modular invariants under the action of $\hbar\rightarrow 0$. Additionally, generalizations of the identities that preserve $\hbar$ are developed which in turn make possible a precise analytical determination of the degeneracies' low-temperature limits in the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda conformal quantum field theory. As an alternative strategy for calculating the degeneracies associated with the most extensively studied Toda conjugate modular invariants, a combination of the character expansions of the integrable highest component Verma modules and the elliptic algebra element $A(x)$ allows for an exact analytical calculation that holds for all temperatures. This approach is further extended to the level 2 Toda modular invariants, where specific relationships known as the extended Ward identities are formulated

The unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) problem, where we assume there's a relationship between source and target data, can be addressed by combining connection network architecture elements with generative adversarial networks. This partnership enables us to evaluate the similarity between the target's distribution and our target-specific generator, using the source data as a reference. This results in a novel method, called relation GAN with triplet loss, that outperforms current state-of-the-art approaches on UDA by effectively integrating these two concepts.

A novel approach for quantum key exchange using twin-field states has been developed, eliminating the need for phase synchronization. Instead of relying on a single source, we've introduced two independent phase sources, one controlled by the two parties, allowing them to efficiently manage their respective phases without requiring coordination. By implementing a distributed randomness protocol in the standard twin-field key exchange method, we've successfully eliminated the dependency on global phase synchronization. Our experimental results verify the effectiveness of this approach and showcase that it can be successfully applied to the level of quantum key distribution. Furthermore, the method has significant potential implications for the scalable implementation of quantum key exchange in quantum networks by leveraging the advantages offered by measurement-depth sharing schemes.

In recent years, object detection using deep learning has become widespread, and lexical knowledge acquisition through object detection has gained significant attention. However, current methods focusing on word recognition encase their ground truth with bounding boxes, making it difficult to merge word and object detection. This paper proposes a novel method to unify word and object detection by introducing a new training technique: training object detection with pseudo box annotations from pre-trained word detectors. We evaluate our approach on the Lexicon-500 dataset and find it outperforms existing methods. Notably, our approach allows the use of smaller datasets more efficiently, as it reduces the required number of annotations by 2.7 times. The improved results and increased robustness demonstrate the merits of this technique.

A large dataset of spectral images spanning X-ray to radio wavelengths has been collected for Rho Ophiuchus, a nearby young stellar object. The dataset reveals that S1, a prominent nebula in Rho Oichi, is surrounded by ionized, atomic, and molecular gas. However, this gas is not in equilibrium, with ionized gas to the north and atomic gas to the south of a curved structure. The curved shape has a 1.5 arcmin radius and is aligned with outflow shocks observed in X-ray. The curved shape is thought to be the result of a 'wind bulb' formed when a young star drives its surrounding material into nearby material. The bulb is pressurized with the material in the center being ionized at around 100,000 Kelvin while the outside material is cooled to around 100 Kelvin. The center of the bulb is also thought to be responsible for the surrounding molecular gas. The material within Rho Oichi is primarily driven by the young star sigma Sco, which has a mass estimated at around 20 solar masses. Based on this estimate, the material in the bulb is on the small side for those driven by typical young stars. The material in the bulb is also thought to be responsible for the surrounding molecular gas. The Transformer model's introduction marked a significant shift from traditional sequence-to-sequence models that heavily relied on recurrent or convolutional neural networks. Initially designed for machine translation by Vaswani et al. in 2017, Transformers have been widely applied in natural language processing tasks such as token classification, sequence classification, and clustering, as well as in areas beyond character encoding, including target detection and unsupervised representation learning, where they have delivered competitive or superior performance compared to conventional architectures. This review provides an overview of the key components of Transformers, their enhancements, and applications in different areas, as well as discussing the challenges and potential future directions. It primarily focuses on the latest advancements in Transformer-based vision models.

The purpose of our study is to assess the performance of portfolio-based models in forecasting individual mortality rates. We compare three approaches: one factor model, two factor models, and a model combining one factor with a time-varying component score based on time-to-event metrics. We trained the models using primary data on male births from the UK and tested them against secondary data from Finland. Our results show that the one factor model and the time-varying component score model exhibit the lowest mean absolute errors in forecasting mortality rates. Additionally, the time-varying component score model demonstrates stability and efficient forecasting capabilities, as its performance is largely unchanged even when using data from a much broader period.

Deep learning models' accuracy can be enhanced by finding an optimal neural architecture. Inspired by the success of random exploration in navigating intricate spaces, researchers have applied novel random architecture search methods in deep learning. Currently, existing random search approaches suffer from disruptions, such as sudden drops in performance, which could be due to two possible reasons - a decline in sampling quality or a sudden transition to extremely poor or extremely excellent architectures. In this study, a novel disruption analysis framework is presented along with an innovative correlation-based criterion to assess sampling quality. Furthermore, a specialized interruption strategy known as correlation-guided interruption is proposed to effectively alleviate disruption. To verify the effectiveness of the proposed techniques, various correlation metrics were evaluated and experimentally confirmed across multiple search spaces, resulting in significant performance gains on ImageNet, with the new methods outperforming state-of-the-art techniques such as random search, COCO-Arch Search, and other established methods by 7.8%, 9.5%, and 11.4% respectively.

Time series data analysis has numerous applications in fields such as weather, finance, and sports. This paper introduces a novel R package named theft, which offers time series anomalies detection through the use of High-Rank Local Correlation and Independent Component Analysis techniques. These methods can be utilized individually or in tandem. The package incorporates two key clustering algorithms: High-Rank Local Correlation and ICA, along with a supporting ElbowPoint function for optimal parameter selection. It also provides HybridClustering, which integrates both techniques, and Distances, a function that computes pairwise distances between time series. The provided case studies showcase the effectiveness of these methods in detecting anomalies and determining the optimal parameter settings. The R code used in these case studies can be found at the theft GitHub repository.

Given a group G and a Coxeter system (S, w), we identify the small bounds
that establish the connection between the growth of G's generating functions and
the dimensions of the associated buildings. Specifically, for a given splitting
of G into a product (H × H'), we find a tight curve that accurately forecasts
the growth of the lengths of shortest paths in the associated building relative to
the lengths of minimal parabolas, under certain diophantine constraints related
to the coefficients defining the splits of (H × H')/H' ∘ H.

Translators are increasingly vital for a range of applications, and effectively utilizing them in practical problems is now a pressing concern. Established evaluation methods for translators have inherent limitations, particularly when applied by inexperienced researchers. A novel approach has been developed, employing Bayesian statistics to quantify the reliability of translators. This systematic method relies on straightforward calculations and a reliable estimate of a translator's error rate in published studies. The proposed method is adaptable to various assessment scenarios, and experiments confirm its efficacy in reliably assessing translator reliability. The experiment also highlighted the challenges posed by unreliable prior estimates, and further research is recommended to establish a database of existing studies assessing translator reliability.

Recent applications of the eigenchannel method, combined with optical theorems, have led to groundbreaking discoveries regarding energy absorption in scattering systems. It was found that the total energy absorbed by a target surrounded by detectors is either limited to its smallest or largest measurement values, multiplied by a constant factor. These constraints demonstrate that the only way to exceed these limits is through non-optimal data collection. These findings aim to facilitate the accurate determination of a system's absorption characteristics from measured data.

This research investigates how different levels of network complexity in the United States affect performance. It challenges the conventional notion that deeper, more complex models require more data to achieve better outcomes. Instead, it argues that sophisticated models have the ability to effectively trim less important connections, much like convolutional networks are capable of doing with respect to fully connected ones. To test this hypothesis, it used a variation of the Neumann et al. trimming technique with a widely used CNN architecture and observed the results. The results revealed that incorporating more data does enhance the performance of such networks. However, when the same models are trained on smaller data sets and their unimportant connections trimmed, they are able to achieve high performance comparable to those trained on larger data sets without trimming taking into account the complexity of the network structure. Additionally, it was observed that deeper networks have a greater capacity to effectively trim less important connections. This research implies that sophisticated models have more resilience and flexibility, which can be a key factor in their ability to succeed.

The concept of predicted value in online marketing, such as advertising and product promotions, is crucial for determining the best approach to achieve optimal results. Essentially, anticipated value represents the average profit gained from a purchase. For online marketers, understanding how to maximize anticipated value can help them streamline their strategies and make more effective decisions. In this paper, we examine the connections between key components of anticipated value - item price, item popularity, and user satisfaction - and explore how they are represented in the Large Graph of the Internet, specifically focusing on the relationships between websites and their vast content. Additionally, we investigate the time-sensitive nature of anticipated value by analyzing variations over time and demonstrate that content categorization can aid in forecasting anticipated value in content-driven markets.

This paper focuses on calculating the $L_2$ norm dimension of the $\phi^Q$ operator where $Q\leq2$, in the context of six-loop $O(N)$ symmetric models. These dimensions are unusual because they are influenced by operator renormalization constants other than $\phi$. Knowledge of these constants is essential to compute the $L_2$ norm dimensions. We determined all required constants at six loops. Crucially, our results differ from a previous study and have significant implications for constructing IR fixed points in relevant theoretical models.

To deepen the understanding of behavioral changes in electrons in 2D materials under external influences, specific calculations were performed using the density functional theory, which considers long-range electrical forces but not all possible interactions between electrons and phonons. It was discovered that the latter plays a more significant role in certain applications and simulations showed that this is particularly true when certain optical processes are involved, which ultimately impact the performance of 2D materials in nano-optical applications and valley-based processing technologies.

The Visual Domain Adjustment Contest, held as part of NeurIPS 2022, tasked participants with developing solutions for an unsupervised problem: mapping images from a set of driving images to a set of target images, with a given set of anchor images serving as references. The goal was to minimize the distance between image embeddings. We successfully solved this problem, taking first place in the contest with our implementation. We then conducted additional experiments to verify the effectiveness of our approach.

t-SNE is a widely employed dimensionality reduction technique that excels in its power to uncover intricate patterns within data sets, particularly in lower dimensional representations. Despite its effectiveness, this method is prone to difficulties when dealing with data that possesses structural characteristics such as alignment or curvature, especially when such properties are significant. In such cases, a spherical distribution of embeddings is beneficial to retain these structural elements. We propose a novel approach, called VMF-SNE, which utilizes the von Mises-Fisher distribution to generate spherical embeddings from input data. We have developed a continuous relaxation for this distribution's lower bounding process and incorporated it into the widely used t-SNE algorithm. By comparing VMF-SNE's performance with state-of-the-art methods such as Weighted SNE, Spherical SNE, and Fast SNE, as well as t-SNE with a symmetrical metric, on a variety of challenging data sets.

Researchers have a keen interest in the polaron regime within the Fermi liquid quasiparticle spectrum due to its occurrence in various key systems including high-temperature superconductors, Bose-Fermi mixtures, and electron-phonon interactions. In this research, a novel white paper is presented to introduce the application of the diagrammatic Monte Carlo technique in the study of polaron phenomena within the Fermi liquid framework in dual dimensions. By leveraging advanced numerical methods developed for fermionic and bosonic systems, recent breakthroughs in the field have demonstrated that the polaron gap can be accurately computed in various coupling strength regimes when employing multiple variational approximations in diagrammatic Monte Carlo. This in turn has facilitated a quantitative understanding of the polaron gap in different many-body states. Nonetheless, a distinct set of challenges arises in the study of the polaron in the context of the Fermi liquid, primarily due to the necessity for diagrammatic Monte Carlo to generate uninterpreted diagrams and thus addressing high-frequency counting issues in a manner that is distinct from conventional many-body theories applying the Matsubara frequency domain. In the context of the Fermi polaron, this is characterized by the requirement for a rapid quasiparticle decay in the direct and indirect veku scales without any ultraviolet cutoff, thereby necessitating a distinct reorganization of the vertices in the many-body spectrum in a manner that is independent of the frequency. Recent advancements in quantum simulation have shed light on the complexities of interacting many-body systems, revealing the reasons behind particular phenomena in near-term quantum computers remain unclear. To address this gap, this work investigates the feasibility of simulating specific fermionic systems using current quantum hardware. The quantum emulation method is first demonstrated with a system of two interacting fermions, revealing the importance of accounting for the inherent digital property of qubits when expressing fermionic Hamiltonians. The impact of analog interactions is identified as the key factor explaining discrepancies between simulations of identical systems on analog and digital quantum computers. Notably, this study also forecasts a significant difference for more complex systems with increased fermions. Furthermore, the digital analog method is found to be applicable to fermionic systems of any finite dimensionality, and its extension to simulate Mott insulators is specifically explored. The simulation of fermionic systems on quantum computers holds great promise for understanding novel materials and interacting systems, and this research plays a crucial role in guiding the optimization of near-term quantum hardware and the development of new quantum applications.

Graph polynomials provide a crucial basis for examining the characteristics of networks. Various graph polynomials have been introduced over the years to address distinct queries. The present study focuses on two widespread families of graph polynomials: the matching polynomials associated with the generating functions of the Hodge numbers of sheaf cohomology of ideal closures, known as $p_{\mathbf{m}}(G)$, and the generalised column polynomials associated with the Hirzebruch coboundary classes, denoted as $p_{\mathbf{c}}(G)$. We aim to explore one-parameter families of graph polynomials that fall within these categories, which can be linked to specific questions involving linear series on curves. Our main real-world application is related to a problem concerning the existence of a specific type of curve with a associated linear series, that connects the genus of a curve to its wheathered projective completion. This leads to several recursive formulas for $p_{\mathbf{c}}(G)$. Furthermore, by utilising $p_{\mathbf{c}}(G)$, we are able to derive alternative methods for calculating the $q$-analogs of the number of non-weakly connected components in a graph, originally introduced by Kirchhoff. The study also provides an in-depth analysis of the theoretical fundamentals underlying the problem with the highest genus, identifying the underlying reasons behind its complexity. We establish a Hitchin relation for the Veech curve in the Teichmüller space of a genus-g fibered surface, which leads to a combinatorial equation involving Capelli elements specific to symplectic representations of the Thompson's group T. Using this relation, we derive an expression for the corresponding pullback of the pullback of the 1-form from Teichmüller space, in terms of integrals of holomorphic 1-forms over the Veech curve for a collection of such forms associated with sympleptic representations of T's action on R^2g.

As the global virus situation persists, the achievement of numerous software engineering research studies remains uncertain due to the shift to remote work. Although some research studies address this shift in general terms, the impact of remote work on the success of specific projects, particularly those managed by Agile methods like Scrum, is a relatively under-investigated topic. To fill this knowledge gap, our study employs both quantitative data analysis and qualitative expert judgment to examine how remote work affects the achievement of Scrum projects. Based on a vast database of open-access papers, our research is distinct from existing studies in its focus on Scrum projects and the application of both quantitative and qualitative methods. A combination of statistical analysis and expert evaluation revealed a link between remote work and the risk of Scum projects failing to meet their objectives. Additionally, our study identifies a potential non-affection of remote work on certain Agile objectives but highlights varying effects on others. Moreover, our research provides guidance to practitioners and stakeholders by identifying the practices that contribute to successful remote work and those that do not. Furthermore, our study proposes a framework to mitigate the challenges of successful Scrum projects in a remote setup. Based on our results, our contribution to the CHIS research field is demonstrated through a formal review process.

The study focused on defining and calculating the Gau-Wu values for selected special types of matrices. Specifically, we investigated four by four arrowhead matrices constructed from the parameters $\lambda_i, i = 1, 2, 3, 4$, which are combinations of real numbers and complex units. To contribute to this area of research, we calculated the Gau-Wu values for a specific class of singular arrowhead matrices. Additionally, we extended our research to include Gau-Wu values for selected general and singular non-arrowhead matrices. Moreover, we demonstrated the potential links between these values and the Gau-Wu polynomials, which are related to the Gau-Wu values.

Our research involves examining electron trajectories resulting from the decay of beauty hadrons created in high-energy Pb-Pb collisions at a specific energy. By studying these electron paths over a wide range of momentum and charge, we analyze how they're influenced by the strong magnetic field generated by the ultrarelativistic collision. Using two distinct methods, we have calculated the size of this magnetic field, which suggests it's comparable to the field strength found in neutron stars. Furthermore, our investigation reveals that beauty hadrons are produced in an elliptical shape within the Albaterni frame, which has significant implications for the understanding of the initial state of the matter created in these collisions. By considering energy-momentum transfer, we have concluded that beauty hadrons are produced predominantly in the transverse plane to the beam axis.

We've developed ComPound PH, a standalone C++ program utilizing GUDLI for computing persistent homology across various dimensions with recent enhancements in color domain handling. ComPound PH incorporates three key methods: quickly generating a delaunay triangulation in 3D, calculating the alpha complexes for a set of colored points in any dimension, and computing persistent homology across different color-based parameters. ComPound PH offers significant flexibility in its point and parameter configurations, allowing users to specify custom colors, weighting schemes, and parameter values via command-line inputs or text files. Additionally, our program includes a point weighting scheme to convert black and white points into a colored format suitable for Delaunay alpha complexes computation. We've also revised our previous color alpha homology definition to incorporate weighted coloring techniques. Moreover, our analysis of artificial and real-world datasets shows ComPound PH's homology persistence persistence graphs resemble the structure of the input points. Examples are provided from our program's usage on a Linux system.
